## Introduction

Modern software systems generate large amounts of telemetry data, including
performance metrics, logs, and other operational signals. This information may
contain early warning signs of system failures; however, detecting those signs
can be challenging, especially in complex systems. Improving failure prediction
can help organizations respond earlier, reduce system downtime and associated
costs, and improve overall system reliability.

This project will use Microsoft's OpenRCA dataset [@xu2025openrca] to
investigate whether Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks can predict
impending software-system failures from system telemetry. Because LSTMs are
designed to learn patterns over time, they may be useful for detecting changes
in telemetry data that occur before a system failure. We will evaluate how
accurately failures can be predicted at different time horizons and whether
combining multiple telemetry sources improves prediction performance compared
with using a single source. Overall, this project applies machine learning to a
practical software reliability problem by testing the effectiveness of telemetry
data for early failure detection.

Previous research is supportive of using LSTM models in the analysis of sequential data.
[@Gonzalez2018] showed that LSTM networks can be used in modeling nonlinear systems,
while [@ErgenKozat2020] used LSTM-based methods for anomaly detection in data sequences
with variable length. Other studies applied LSTMs to telemetry data obtained from computer
systems. [@MudgalWouhaybi2024] used a combined LSTM encoder in anomaly detection methods.
These include Isolation Forest, used to identify PC system failures from CPU, memory, disk,
temperature, and system data. This study obtained results that suggested LSTM-based telemetry
analysis can provide useful results for system-failure detection.

System log research also shows how important sequential modeling can be in failure-related
tasks. [@Chen2022] used two LSTM networks in the analysis of events before and after a log
entry; this improved anomaly detection in long log sequences. In addition, [@Hadadi2024]
researched deep learning for log-based failure prediction and found that model performance is
dependent on how log data are represented and transformed into sequences. The OpenRCA dataset
will be particularly useful in this project as it contains real failure case data from enterprise
systems, with multiple sources of telemetry, such as logs, metrics, and traces [@Xu2025].
While the prior work mentioned mainly focused on anomaly detection or cause analysis, this
project will be more focused on predicting failures before they occur and testing the efficacy
of multiple telemetry sources in improving early failure prediction performance.

## Methods

A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is a type of recurrent neural network (RNN)
designed to learn from sequential data while retaining useful information over time.
As it processes each time step, the LSTM updates a cell state that carries information
forward. Three gates control this process: the forget gate determines what information
to retain, the input gate determines what new information to add, and the output gate
determines what information to expose to the next time step. This gating structure
helps the network learn which patterns of change over time are useful for making
predictions [@Hochreiter1997].

We chose an LSTM because it can learn from the order of telemetry measurements over
time. Some faults may be preceded by gradual changes in metrics, such as increasing
memory use or CPU utilization that remains elevated. By processing a recent sequence
of measurements, the model can learn whether these patterns help predict a fault before
it begins. This section explains how the LSTM processes sequences, the assumptions
behind our modeling approach, how we prepare OpenRCA telemetry for the model, and how
we train it.

### Recurrent Neural Networks and the Vanishing Gradient

A recurrent neural network processes a sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_T$ one step at
a time. At each step it combines the current input $x_t$ with a *hidden state*
$h_{t-1}$ that summarizes everything it has seen so far:

$$
h_t = \tanh\left(W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b\right)
$$ {#eq-rnn}

The same weights $W$, $U$ and $b$ are reused at every time step, so the network can
handle a sequence of any length with a fixed number of parameters.

RNNs are trained with *backpropagation through time* (BPTT) [@Werbos1990]: the
network is "unrolled" over the sequence, and the error at the final step is passed
backwards through every earlier step. The gradient that reaches step $t-k$ contains
a product of $k$ Jacobian matrices,

$$
\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-k}} = \prod_{j=t-k+1}^{t} \operatorname{diag}\!\left(1 - h_j^2\right) U .
$$ {#eq-bptt}

When the terms in this product are smaller than one, the gradient shrinks
exponentially as $k$ grows (it *vanishes*); when they are larger than one, it grows
exponentially (it *explodes*) [@Bengio1994; @Pascanu2013]. In practice, a plain RNN
therefore learns only short-range patterns. For our problem, this is a serious
limitation: an early warning sign 20 minutes before a fault is 20 steps back in the
sequence.

### Mathematical Foundations of the LSTM

The LSTM replaces the single update in @eq-rnn with a memory cell $c_t$ and three
gates. Following the standard formulation with a forget gate [@Gers2000], the
computation at each time step $t$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_t &= \sigma\left(W_f x_t + U_f h_{t-1} + b_f\right) && \text{forget gate}\\
i_t &= \sigma\left(W_i x_t + U_i h_{t-1} + b_i\right) && \text{input gate}\\
o_t &= \sigma\left(W_o x_t + U_o h_{t-1} + b_o\right) && \text{output gate}\\
\tilde{c}_t &= \tanh\left(W_c x_t + U_c h_{t-1} + b_c\right) && \text{candidate memory}\\
c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t && \text{cell state update}\\
h_t &= o_t \odot \tanh\left(c_t\right) && \text{hidden state (output)}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-lstm}

where:

- $x_t$ is the input vector at time $t$: the telemetry readings for one minute.
- $h_{t-1}$ is the hidden state from the previous minute; $h_t$ is the new one.
- $c_{t-1}$ and $c_t$ are the old and new **cell states**: the long-term memory.
- $f_t$, $i_t$, $o_t$ are the **gates**. Each is a vector of numbers between 0 and 1
  produced by the logistic sigmoid $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$. A value near 0 means
  "block" and a value near 1 means "let through".
- $\tilde{c}_t$ is the **candidate memory**: new information that could be written
  to the cell. The $\tanh$ function keeps it between $-1$ and $1$.
- $W_\ast$ are the input weight matrices, $U_\ast$ are the recurrent weight matrices, 
  and $b_\ast$ are bias vectors, one set for each gate and the candidate.
- $\odot$ is element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication.

**What each gate does.**

- The **forget gate** $f_t$ decides how much of the old memory $c_{t-1}$ to keep.
  If a component of $f_t$ is close to 1, that part of the memory is carried forward;
  close to 0, it is erased.
- The **input gate** $i_t$ decides how much of the candidate $\tilde{c}_t$ is written
  into memory. This lets the network ignore minutes that carry no useful information.
- The **output gate** $o_t$ decides how much of the memory is exposed in the hidden
  state $h_t$, which is what the next step, and eventually the prediction layer,
  sees.

**Why this fixes the vanishing gradient.** The key line in @eq-lstm is the cell
update $c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t$. It is *additive*, not a
repeated squashing like @eq-rnn. Along this path, the gradient from one step to the
previous is

$$
\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} \approx \operatorname{diag}(f_t),
$$

so as long as the network learns to keep the forget gate open ($f_t \approx 1$), the
error signal can travel back across many time steps without shrinking. This is the
"constant error carousel" that gives the LSTM its long memory [@Hochreiter1997].

#### Matrix and Vector Dimensions

Let $k$ be the number of input features and $d$ the number of hidden units. Then:

| Symbol | Dimension | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_t$ | $k \times 1$ | telemetry at minute $t$ |
| $h_t,\; c_t,\; f_t,\; i_t,\; o_t,\; \tilde{c}_t$ | $d \times 1$ | hidden state, cell state, gates, candidate |
| $W_f, W_i, W_o, W_c$ | $d \times k$ | input weights |
| $U_f, U_i, U_o, U_c$ | $d \times d$ | recurrent weights |
| $b_f, b_i, b_o, b_c$ | $d \times 1$ | biases |

The four weight sets are usually stacked into one matrix, so a single LSTM layer has

$$
4\left(dk + d^2 + d\right)
$$

trainable parameters. In this project, the input has $k = 128$ selected telemetry
features and the LSTM has $d = 64$ hidden units, which gives
$4(64 \cdot 128 + 64^2 + 64) = 49{,}408$ parameters in the LSTM layer. (PyTorch keeps
two bias vectors per gate, which adds another $4d = 256$.) The prediction layer
described below adds $d + 1 = 65$ more, for a total of $49{,}729$ parameters.
Importantly, this number does not depend on the length of the sequence: the same
weights are applied at every minute.

#### Example

To make @eq-lstm concrete, consider a toy LSTM with $d = 1$ hidden unit that watches
$k = 2$ scaled telemetry features of one container: CPU usage and memory usage. At
the previous minute, the network's state was $h_{t-1} = 0.2$ and $c_{t-1} = 0.5$. At
the current minute, CPU usage spikes while memory is normal:

$$
x_t = \begin{bmatrix} \text{CPU} \\ \text{Memory} \end{bmatrix}
    = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 \\ 0.3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Suppose training has produced the following weights:

| Gate | $W_\ast$ (CPU, Memory) | $U_\ast$ | $b_\ast$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| forget $f$ | $[\,0.6,\; -0.2\,]$ | 0.5 | 1.0 |
| input $i$ | $[\,0.8,\; 0.1\,]$ | 0.3 | 0.0 |
| output $o$ | $[\,0.4,\; 0.2\,]$ | 0.6 | 0.2 |
| candidate $\tilde{c}$ | $[\,0.9,\; 0.3\,]$ | 0.4 | $-0.1$ |

**Step 1: gates.** For the forget gate,

$$
f_t = \sigma(0.6 \cdot 1.5 - 0.2 \cdot 0.3 + 0.5 \cdot 0.2 + 1.0) = \sigma(1.94) = 0.874 .
$$

The other gates follow in the same way:

$$
i_t = \sigma(1.29) = 0.784, \qquad
o_t = \sigma(0.98) = 0.727, \qquad
\tilde{c}_t = \tanh(1.42) = 0.890 .
$$

**Step 2: update the memory.**

$$
c_t = \underbrace{0.874 \times 0.5}_{\text{kept from before}}
    + \underbrace{0.784 \times 0.890}_{\text{newly written}}
    = 0.437 + 0.698 = 1.135
$$

**Step 3: produce the output.**

$$
h_t = 0.727 \times \tanh(1.135) = 0.727 \times 0.813 = 0.591
$$

The network kept most of its earlier memory (87 %) and added a large new
contribution because the CPU spike opened the input gate. The value of $c_t$ has
grown from 0.5 to 1.135, so the "something unusual is happening" signal will be
carried into the next minutes. Repeating these three steps for every minute of
the look-back window is all the LSTM does; training consists of finding weights
that make this memory useful for predicting failures.

#### From a Sequence to a Failure Prediction

For each minute $t$ we give the LSTM the previous $L = 60$ minutes of telemetry,
$x_{t-59}, \dots, x_t$, and run @eq-lstm over them in order. Only the final hidden
state $h_t$ is used for the prediction, because by then it summarizes the whole
window. It passes through dropout and a single linear layer, and a sigmoid turns
the result into a probability:

$$
\hat{p}_t = \sigma\!\left(v^{\top} \operatorname{Dropout}(h_t) + b_v\right),
$$ {#eq-head}

where $v$ is a $d \times 1$ weight vector and $b_v$ is a scalar. $\hat{p}_t$ is the
model's estimated probability that a failure will start within the next $H$ minutes.

![The LSTM unrolled over a 60-minute look-back window. The same cell (same weights) is applied every minute; only the final hidden state feeds the prediction.](figures/lstm_unrolled.svg){#fig-unrolled width="100%"}

### Parameter Estimation

The parameters $\theta = \{W_\ast, U_\ast, b_\ast, v, b_v\}$ are learned by minimizing
a **weighted binary cross-entropy** loss over the $N$ training windows:

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}
\Big[\, w_{+}\, y_n \log \hat{p}_n + (1 - y_n)\log\left(1 - \hat{p}_n\right) \Big]
$$ {#eq-loss}

where $y_n \in \{0, 1\}$ is the true label. Failures are rare, so the positive-class
weight $w_{+}$ is set to the ratio of negative to positive windows in the training
data. Without this weight the model could reach a low loss by always predicting
"no failure".

Gradients of @eq-loss are computed by backpropagation through time and the weights
are updated with the **Adam** optimizer [@Kingma2015], which adapts the step size for
each parameter. Several standard techniques keep training stable and reduce
overfitting:

- **Gradient clipping.** If the overall gradient norm exceeds 5 it is rescaled to 5.
  This guards against the exploding-gradient problem described above [@Pascanu2013].
- **Dropout** with rate 0.2 on the final hidden state randomly zeroes units during
  training, so the prediction cannot rely on any single unit [@Srivastava2014].
- **Weight decay** of $10^{-5}$ adds a small L2 penalty on the weights.
- **Early stopping.** After each epoch the model is scored on a separate validation
  set. Training stops when the validation score has not improved for 4 epochs, and
  the weights from the best epoch are restored.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Look-back window $L$ | 60 minutes |
| Input features $k$ | 128 |
| Hidden units $d$ | 64 |
| LSTM layers | 1 |
| Dropout | 0.2 |
| Optimizer | Adam, learning rate $10^{-3}$, weight decay $10^{-5}$ |
| Batch size | 128 |
| Maximum epochs | 15 |
| Early-stopping patience | 4 epochs (on validation PR-AUC) |
| Gradient clipping | max norm 5 |

: Default LSTM configuration. {#tbl-config}

## Analysis and Results

### Dataset Description

The data come from **OpenRCA** [@xu2025openrca], a public benchmark released by
Microsoft for root-cause analysis of software failures. OpenRCA collects telemetry
from three enterprise microservice systems: **Bank**, **Telecom** and **Market**
(the last split into two deployments, `cloudbed-1` and `cloudbed-2`), into which
engineers deliberately injected faults such as CPU exhaustion, memory leaks and
network delays. For every system, OpenRCA provides:

- **Telemetry**, organised into one folder per day, with three modalities:
  - **metrics**: numeric key performance indicators (KPIs) such as CPU use, memory
    use, response time, and request counts, sampled every few seconds to minutes;
  - **logs**: text messages written by the services;
  - **traces**: records of individual requests travelling between services.
- **A fault record** (`record.csv`) listing every injected fault with its start
  time, the component it was injected into, and the type of fault.

**Scope of this study.** We focus on the **Bank** and **Telecom** systems and on their
**metric** telemetry only. We chose these two systems because:

1. Each is a single, self-contained system with one fault record, so the telemetry
   and the labels line up directly. Market is split into two separate deployments
   that would each need their own pipeline.
2. They are very different from each other (different business domains, numbers of
   components, monitoring tools and time periods), so a result that holds on both
   is more convincing than a result on one.
3. Metrics are numeric time series that can be placed on a common one-minute grid,
   which is the input the LSTM needs. Logs and traces would first require text
   parsing and request-level aggregation, which is outside the scope of this project.

| | **Bank** | **Telecom** |
|---|---|---|
| Domain | Online banking platform | Telecom operator services |
| Recorded days | 10 (2021-03-04 to 2021-03-25, not consecutive) | 15 (2020-04-11 to 2020-05-31, not consecutive) |
| Telemetry per day | 24 hours (1,440 minutes) | 6 hours, 00:00–05:59 (360 minutes) |
| Total minutes | 14,400 | 5,400 |
| Metric files per day | `metric_container.csv`, `metric_app.csv` | `metric_node.csv`, `metric_container.csv`, `metric_middleware.csv`, `metric_service.csv`, `metric_app.csv` |
| Timestamp unit | seconds | milliseconds |
| Injected faults | 136 | 51 |
| Fault types | 8 | 5 |

: Overview of the two OpenRCA systems used in this study. {#tbl-systems}

All OpenRCA timestamps are Unix epoch values, and all dates and day-folder names are
in **UTC+8** (China Standard Time). Dates and times in this report are shown in UTC+8.

#### Variable Description

The **fault record** has the same columns in both systems:

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `level` | Level of the system where the fault was injected: `pod` (a container), `node` (a host machine) or `service`. All Bank faults are at pod level. |
| `component` | Name of the component the fault was injected into, for example `Mysql02` (Bank) or `docker_003` (Telecom). |
| `timestamp` | Fault start time as a Unix epoch value (seconds). |
| `datetime` | The same start time written as a date and time in UTC+8. |
| `reason` | Type of fault, for example `high CPU usage` or `network delay`. |

: Columns of `record.csv`. {#tbl-record-vars}

The record gives each fault's **start time only**; it does not say how long the fault
lasted. This is important for labeling, described below.

The **metric files** come in two layouts:

| Layout | Files | Columns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long (one row per reading) | Bank `metric_container.csv`; all Telecom files except `metric_app.csv` | `timestamp`, `cmdb_id`, `kpi_name` / `name`, `value` | At time `timestamp`, KPI `kpi_name` on component `cmdb_id` had value `value`. |
| Wide (one row per service per time) | Bank and Telecom `metric_app.csv` | Bank: `timestamp`, `tc`, `rr`, `sr`, `cnt`, `mrt`; Telecom: `startTime`, `serviceName`, `avg_time`, `num`, `succee_num`, `succee_rate` | Application-level request statistics: request count, success rate and mean response time per service. |

: Layouts of the metric files. {#tbl-metric-layout}

Each combination of a component and a KPI, for example `Tomcat04 ‖ CPU utilisation`,
is one **time series**, and becomes one input feature for the model.

### Packages

The analysis uses two languages. Python prepares the telemetry and trains the model,
because the data are large and the LSTM is built with PyTorch. R reads the saved
results and produces the tables and figures in this report.

**Python**

- **pandas** and **pyarrow**: read the metric CSV files, pivot them into
  minute-by-feature tables and store them as Parquet files.
- **NumPy**: cleaning, scaling, windowing and the evaluation metrics (PR-AUC, ROC-AUC,
  bootstrap intervals).
- **PyTorch** [@Paszke2019]: defines the LSTM, computes gradients by backpropagation
  through time and trains the model with Adam.

**R**

- **tidyverse** (readr, dplyr, tidyr, purrr, stringr, ggplot2): read the results,
  reshape them and draw the figures.
- **knitr**: format tables.
- **scales**: format percentages.

### Load Data

```{r, warning=FALSE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE}
# loading packages
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
```

The fault records are small and are loaded directly. Start times are converted from
epoch seconds to UTC+8 date-times.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
read_record <- function(path, system) {
  read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    transmute(system    = system,
              level,
              component,
              reason,
              timestamp = as.numeric(timestamp),
              onset     = as.POSIXct(timestamp, origin = "1970-01-01",
                                     tz = "Asia/Shanghai"))   # UTC+8
}

faults <- bind_rows(
  read_record("data/bank_record.csv",    "Bank"),
  read_record("data/telecom_record.csv", "Telecom")
)

faults |>
  group_by(system) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  select(system, level, component, reason, onset) |>
  kable(caption = "First three faults in each system's record.")
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
faults |>
  count(system, reason, name = "faults") |>
  group_by(system) |>
  mutate(share = scales::percent(faults / sum(faults), accuracy = 1)) |>
  arrange(system, desc(faults)) |>
  kable(caption = "Injected fault types by system.")
```

Both systems are dominated by a few fault types. In Bank, high CPU usage, network
packet loss and network latency make up two-thirds of all faults, while JVM CPU load
(3 faults) and disk space (5 faults) are too rare to evaluate on their own. In
Telecom, CPU faults and network delay make up 63 %.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
faults |>
  mutate(day = as.Date(onset, tz = "Asia/Shanghai")) |>
  count(system, day, name = "faults") |>
  group_by(system) |>
  summarise(days_with_faults = n(),
            min_per_day      = min(faults),
            max_per_day      = max(faults),
            total            = sum(faults)) |>
  kable(caption = "Faults per day.")
```

Bank has faults on 9 of its 10 days and Telecom on 11 of its 15 days. The days with
telemetry but **no recorded faults** (Bank 2021-03-05; Telecom 2020-04-20 to
2020-04-23) are kept in the data as fault-free periods.

The metric telemetry is much larger (about 16 GB for Telecom and roughly 90 MB per
day for Bank), so it is not stored in this repository. It is read day by day in Python
with pandas. The function below reads one metric file and turns it into a table with
one row per minute and one column per `component‖KPI` series; the long and wide
layouts in @tbl-metric-layout are handled separately:

```python
def load_source(day_dir, src, grid):
    """Read one metric file into a minute x feature table ('component||kpi')."""
    if src.kind == "long":
        df = pd.read_csv(day_dir / src.path,
                         usecols=[src.ts_col, src.id_col, src.kpi_col, src.val_col])
        df["minute"] = to_minute(df[src.ts_col], src.ts_unit)   # s or ms -> minute
        df["feature"] = df[src.id_col] + "||" + df[src.kpi_col]
        wide = df.pivot_table(index="minute", columns="feature",
                              values=src.val_col, aggfunc="mean")
    else:  # wide layout (metric_app.csv)
        df = pd.read_csv(day_dir / src.path)
        df["minute"] = to_minute(df[src.ts_col], src.ts_unit)
        wide = pd.concat([df.pivot_table(index="minute", columns=src.id_col,
                                         values=v, aggfunc="mean")
                            .add_prefix("app||").add_suffix("." + v)
                          for v in src.value_cols], axis=1)
    return wide.reindex(grid)          # exact 1-minute grid for that day
```

Running this for every metric file and every day produces the raw feature tables:

| | **Bank** | **Telecom** |
|---|---|---|
| Rows (minutes) | 14,400 | 5,400 |
| Components in the telemetry | 18 | 51 |
| Raw `component‖KPI` series | 1,933 | 2,073 |
| Cells missing in the raw 1-minute grid | 48.3 % | 25.5 % |

: Size of the raw feature tables after loading. {#tbl-raw}

The high share of missing cells is expected: many KPIs are recorded every 2 minutes
or once an hour rather than every minute, so most of their cells on a 1-minute grid
are empty.

### Data Preparation and Labeling

#### Cleaning the telemetry

The raw tables are cleaned in four steps. To avoid leaking information from the
test period, steps 2–4 are **fitted on the training days only** and then applied
unchanged to the validation and test days. They are re-fitted for every
train/test split; the numbers below are for the chronological split used in the
Modeling and Results section.

1. **Align to a 1-minute grid.** Every reading is assigned to the minute it falls in,
   and readings within the same minute are averaged. Each day becomes exactly 1,440
   (Bank) or 360 (Telecom) rows. Telecom timestamps are first divided by 1,000 to
   convert milliseconds to seconds. This step looks only at each reading's own
   timestamp, so it learns nothing from the data.
2. **Keep only series observed on every training day.** A model cannot learn from a
   feature that is missing for whole training days. In Bank this removes mainly the
   containers `dockerA1`, `dockerA2`, `dockerB1` and `dockerB2`, which report only
   intermittently. If a kept series is missing on a test day, it is treated like any
   other gap (step 4).
3. **Drop sparse series.** Any series more than 80 % missing on the training days is
   removed; there is too little data to fill it reliably.
4. **Fill gaps using past values only.** Within each day, a missing value is filled
   with the last observed value, for up to twice that series' sampling interval
   (estimated on the training days) and at least 2 minutes. A KPI sampled every
   2 minutes can therefore be filled for up to 4 minutes, while a longer outage is not
   hidden. Values are never filled backwards from a later reading, and never across
   days, so each minute only uses information available at that minute. Any gap that
   remains is set to the series' training median.

| | **Bank** | **Telecom** |
|---|---|---|
| Raw series | 1,933 | 2,073 |
| Removed: not observed on every training day | 248 | 421 |
| Removed: more than 80 % missing on training days | 118 | 421 |
| **Features kept** | **1,567** | **1,231** |
| Missing cells after forward-filling, training days | 1.1 % | 1.2 % |
| Missing cells after forward-filling, all days | 4.9 % | 1.4 % |

: Effect of each cleaning step, fitted on the training days of the chronological split. {#tbl-cleaning}

The remaining gaps are more common on the Bank test days than on its training days,
which is an early sign that the test period behaves differently.

#### Labeling

The fault record gives a start time for each fault, but our goal is to predict a
fault *before* it starts. We therefore turn each fault into labels on the minutes
leading up to it. For a prediction horizon of $H$ minutes, the label of minute $t$ is

$$
y_{t,H} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if any fault starts in the interval } (t,\; t + H],\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-label}

In words, minute $t$ is positive if a failure will begin within the next $H$
minutes. We build labels for six horizons, $H \in \{1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 30\}$ minutes,
so we can measure how prediction quality changes as the model is asked to look
further ahead. Fault start times are rounded down to the minute so that they fall on
the same grid as the telemetry. All 136 Bank and 51 Telecom faults land on the grid.

Two further rules decide which minutes can be used at all:

- **Blackout after a fault.** The record does not say how long a fault lasts. For the
  10 minutes after a fault starts, the system is probably still failing, so these
  minutes are removed from the negative examples. Otherwise the model would be
  rewarded for "predicting" a fault that is already visible in the telemetry.
- **Complete windows only.** A minute is used only if its full 60-minute look-back
  window *and* its $H$-minute look-ahead both lie on the same day. The recorded days
  are not consecutive; for example, Bank jumps from 2021-03-12 to 2021-03-23, so a
  window that crossed midnight would join two unrelated days together.

These rules remove the first hour of every day and a few minutes around each fault.
@tbl-positive shows the result: the number of usable minutes and the share labelled
positive at each horizon.

| $H$ (min) | Bank positive / usable | Bank rate | Telecom positive / usable | Telecom rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 129 / 12,382 | 1.04 % | 42 / 4,033 | 1.04 % |
| 3 | 386 / 12,370 | 3.12 % | 126 / 4,003 | 3.15 % |
| 5 | 642 / 12,363 | 5.19 % | 210 / 3,974 | 5.28 % |
| 10 | 1,279 / 12,358 | 10.35 % | 420 / 3,904 | 10.76 % |
| 15 | 1,902 / 12,368 | 15.38 % | 630 / 3,839 | 16.41 % |
| 30 | 3,573 / 12,459 | 28.68 % | 1,217 / 3,812 | 31.93 % |

: Positive minutes by prediction horizon. {#tbl-positive}

Three points stand out:

- **Positives are rare at short horizons.** At $H = 1$ only about 1 % of minutes are
  positive. A model that always predicts "no failure" would be 99 % accurate, which
  is why we evaluate with PR-AUC rather than accuracy.
- **The two systems are directly comparable.** Both have about 9.4 faults per 1,000
  minutes, so their positive rates are almost identical at every horizon.
- **The real sample size is the number of faults.** Positive minutes next to each
  other belong to the same fault and are not independent. Bank has 136 fault events
  and Telecom only 51, so Telecom results will be less certain.

### Data Exploration and Visualization

```{r, echo=TRUE}
eda <- function(system, file)
  read_csv(file.path("results", system, "eda", file), show_col_types = FALSE)
recorded_days <- function(system)
  read_csv(file.path("results", system, "chrono-level", "split.csv"),
           show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(horizon == 1) |> pull(days) |> str_split(", ") |> unlist() |> as.Date()
```

#### When faults happen

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.4}
#| label: fig-faults-per-day
#| fig-cap: "Injected faults per recorded day. Days are shown in order with gaps removed; days with no bar have telemetry but no recorded faults."
per_day <- bind_rows(
  tibble(system = "Bank",    day = recorded_days("bank")),
  tibble(system = "Telecom", day = recorded_days("telecom"))) |>
  left_join(faults |> mutate(day = as.Date(onset, tz = "Asia/Shanghai")) |>
              count(system, day, name = "faults"), by = c("system", "day")) |>
  mutate(faults = replace_na(faults, 0L), label = format(day, "%m-%d"))

ggplot(per_day, aes(label, faults)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_text(aes(label = faults), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~system, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Faults") +
  theme_bw() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Faults are spread fairly evenly over the Bank days (10 to 21 a day), apart from
2021-03-05, which has full telemetry but no faults. Telecom is uneven: one fault-heavy
day in April, four fault-free days in a row (04-20 to 04-23), and then 2 to 8 faults a
day in late May. Because faults are injected about once an hour in both systems, a
60-minute look-back window before one fault often contains the aftermath of the
previous one.

#### How complete the telemetry is

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.4}
#| label: fig-missingness
#| fig-cap: "Share of missing minutes per series, on the raw 1-minute grid and after cleaning (series kept for the chronological split, after forward-filling)."
bind_rows(Bank = eda("bank", "missingness.csv"),
          Telecom = eda("telecom", "missingness.csv"), .id = "system") |>
  pivot_longer(c(raw, after_cleaning), names_to = "stage", values_to = "missing") |>
  filter(!is.na(missing)) |>
  mutate(stage = recode(stage, raw = "Raw 1-minute grid",
                        after_cleaning = "After cleaning")) |>
  ggplot(aes(missing, fill = stage)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6, boundary = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~system, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Raw 1-minute grid" = "#009E73", "After cleaning" = "#CC79A7")) +
  labs(x = "Share of minutes missing", y = "Series", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

On the raw 1-minute grid most Bank series are 20 % to 70 % missing. This is a
sampling effect, not data loss: many Bank KPIs are recorded every 2 minutes or once an
hour. Telecom series are either almost complete or mostly empty. After cleaning, the
kept series are nearly complete (Bank 4.9 %, Telecom 1.4 % of cells still missing),
so the LSTM sees a regular grid as the Methods section assumes.

#### What the telemetry looks like around a fault

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5}
#| label: fig-closeup
#| fig-cap: "Four KPIs of the faulty component around one fault in each system, scaled to 0 to 1 over the window shown. The vertical line is the recorded fault start."
bind_rows(eda("bank", "closeup.csv"), eda("telecom", "closeup.csv")) |>
  mutate(panel = paste0(component, ", ", reason, " (", onset, ")"),
         kpi = str_remove(kpi, "^OSLinux-OSLinux_|^container\\.")) |>
  ggplot(aes(minute, value, colour = kpi)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Minutes relative to fault start", y = "Scaled value", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))
```

The two close-ups show why single examples are hard to read. On Bank server `MG01`,
filesystem metrics grow steadily through the 30 minutes before a "high memory usage"
fault, which at first looks like a warning sign. But they keep growing at the same
pace for the hour after it, so the growth is more likely a steady trend, such as a
disk filling up, than a sign of this fault. The memory metrics themselves do not move,
so the label describes what was injected, not where it shows up. On Telecom container
`docker_004`, CPU and memory use jump about two minutes after the recorded fault start
and stay high for about six minutes. A similar CPU burst about 20 minutes earlier
returns to normal without a fault, so it is unclear whether such bursts are warnings
or noise.

#### Does the telemetry change before faults in general?

To look beyond single examples, we measured how much the telemetry moves around
every fault. For each fault with at least 60 minutes of history on the same day, each
feature is compared with its own median 31 to 60 minutes before the fault, in units
of its training IQR, and the absolute change is averaged over all features. The same
is done at 200 to 300 randomly chosen times at least 90 minutes away from any fault.
This gives 126 fault windows for Bank and 40 for Telecom.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.6}
#| label: fig-onset-profile
#| fig-cap: "Average change in the telemetry relative to a baseline 31 to 60 minutes earlier, around fault starts and around random fault-free times. Ribbons are 95 % confidence intervals across windows."
bind_rows(Bank = eda("bank", "onset_profile.csv"),
          Telecom = eda("telecom", "onset_profile.csv"), .id = "system") |>
  mutate(kind = recode(kind, fault = "Around a fault start",
                       random = "Random fault-free time")) |>
  group_by(system, kind, minute) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(change), se = sd(change) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(minute, mean, colour = kind, fill = kind)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
              alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~system, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Minutes relative to fault start (or random time)",
       y = "Mean |change| (training IQRs)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
bind_rows(Bank = eda("bank", "onset_profile.csv"),
          Telecom = eda("telecom", "onset_profile.csv"), .id = "System") |>
  filter(kind == "fault") |>
  mutate(period = case_when(minute < -30 ~ "base",
                            minute < 0 ~ "pre",
                            minute <= 5 ~ "onset",
                            TRUE ~ "later")) |>
  group_by(System, reason, period) |>
  summarise(change = mean(change), n = n_distinct(onset), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = change) |>
  transmute(System, `Fault type` = reason, Faults = n,
            `Last 30 min before start` = sprintf("%+.3f", pre - base),
            `First 5 min after start` = sprintf("%+.3f", onset - base)) |>
  arrange(System, desc(Faults)) |>
  kable(caption = "Average telemetry change by fault type, relative to 31 to 60 minutes before the fault (training IQRs).")
```

@fig-onset-profile shows the central fact about these data. In both systems the
telemetry around faults is somewhat busier than at quiet times throughout the hour
(faults are injected about once an hour, so earlier faults are still settling), but
the gap between the two curves **does not grow in the minutes before a fault**. It
widens only at the fault start: in Bank the average change rises from about 0.60 in
the last minutes before the start to about 0.68 in the first minutes after it, and in
Telecom from about 0.55 to about 0.62, while the random-time curves only drift up
slowly as the distance from their baseline grows.

The table breaks this down by fault type. Every type with more than three faults
changes the telemetry more in the first 5 minutes after its start than in the 30
minutes before it. The fault types with the largest pre-onset change are
Bank's "high disk space usage" and "network packet loss", but even there the change
in the 30 minutes before the start is smaller than in the 5 minutes after it.

#### Unexpected patterns

- **Fault-free days.** Bank 2021-03-05 and Telecom 2020-04-20 to 04-23 have complete
  telemetry but no recorded faults. They may be quiet periods or gaps in the fault
  record; the dataset does not say which. Either way, they make some days look very
  different from others in their share of positive minutes.
- **Slow trends across days.** Some metrics, such as disk usage on the Bank `IG`
  servers, grow steadily over the recording. Such a metric separates early days from
  late days, and therefore days with few faults from days with many, without saying
  anything about the minutes before a particular fault.
- **Labels describe the injection, not the symptom.** The "high memory usage" fault in
  @fig-closeup does not show up in the memory metrics of the faulty server, which
  argues for a model that can use all features rather than a hand-picked few.
- **Telecom covers only 00:00 to 05:59.** Every Telecom minute is in the early
  morning, so its daily load pattern differs from Bank's 24-hour days.

These observations set expectations for the model: if the telemetry rarely changes
before a fault, an LSTM, however good at remembering the past, has little to work
with, and slow day-level trends may be the strongest signal available to it.

### Modeling and Results

We apply the same model and the same procedure to both systems. Bank is analysed
first because it has the most fault events (136) and full 24-hour days; Telecom (51
events, 6 hours a day) then shows whether the findings carry over to a different
system.

The LSTM is trained in Python with PyTorch. The scripts are in the `code/` folder of
this repository and their outputs in `results/<system>/`; the report reads the saved
results, so rendering it does not retrain the model.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
res <- function(system, run, file)
  read_csv(file.path("results", system, run, file), show_col_types = FALSE)
pct <- function(x, d = 1) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 10^-d)

show_metrics <- function(system, run) {
  alarmed <- res(system, run, "predictions.csv") |>
    group_by(horizon) |> summarise(alarmed = mean(alarm))
  res(system, run, "metrics.csv") |>
    left_join(alarmed, by = "horizon") |>
    transmute(`H (min)` = horizon,
              `Base rate` = round(base_rate, 3),
              `PR-AUC [95 % CI]` = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", pr_auc, pr_auc_lo, pr_auc_hi),
              Lift = sprintf("%.2f", pr_lift),
              `ROC-AUC` = round(roc_auc, 3),
              `Minutes alarmed` = pct(alarmed),
              `Faults caught` = sprintf("%d / %d", events_detected, n_events),
              `False alarms / day` = round(false_alarms_per_day, 1))
}

plot_history <- function(system) {
  res(system, "chrono-level", "history.csv") |>
    mutate(H = factor(paste0("H = ", horizon),
                      levels = paste0("H = ", c(1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 30)))) |>
    pivot_longer(c(train_loss, val_pr_auc), names_to = "metric") |>
    mutate(metric = recode(metric, train_loss = "Training loss",
                           val_pr_auc = "Validation PR-AUC")) |>
    ggplot(aes(epoch, value, colour = H)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, epoch == best_epoch & metric == "Validation PR-AUC")) +
    facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(x = "Epoch", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
    theme_bw()
}

plot_timeline <- function(system, sys_name, test_start, h = 5) {
  pred <- res(system, "chrono-level", "predictions.csv") |> filter(horizon == h) |>
    mutate(time = as.POSIXct(timestamp, origin = "1970-01-01", tz = "Asia/Shanghai"),
           day  = format(time, "%m-%d"))
  thr <- res(system, "chrono-level", "metrics.csv") |> filter(horizon == h) |> pull(threshold)
  onsets <- faults |>
    filter(system == sys_name,
           as.Date(onset, tz = "Asia/Shanghai") >= as.Date(test_start)) |>
    mutate(day = format(onset, "%m-%d"))
  ggplot(pred, aes(time, score)) +
    geom_vline(data = onsets, aes(xintercept = onset), colour = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_line(colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = thr, linetype = "dashed") +
    facet_wrap(~day, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
    scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M") +
    labs(x = "Time (UTC+8)", y = "Predicted probability") +
    theme_bw()
}

plot_drift <- function(system, strip) {
  drift <- read_csv(file.path("results", system, "drift.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(feature = str_replace(feature, strip, ": "),
           label = format(as.Date(day), "%m-%d"),
           x = as.integer(factor(label)))
  days <- distinct(drift, x, label, split)
  ggplot(drift, aes(x, scaled_mean, colour = feature)) +
    geom_rect(data = days,
              aes(xmin = x - 0.5, xmax = x + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = split),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.15) +
    geom_line() + geom_point() +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = days$x, labels = days$label) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(train = "grey60", val = "#E69F00", test = "#D55E00")) +
    labs(x = "Day (recorded days only)", y = "Daily mean (training IQRs)",
         colour = NULL, fill = "Split") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical",
          axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
}

runs <- c("chrono-level"  = "Chronological, level",
          "chrono-change" = "Chronological, change",
          "cv-level"      = "Cross-validation, level",
          "cv-change"     = "Cross-validation, change")

plot_lift <- function(system) {
  imap_dfr(runs, \(lab, run) res(system, run, "metrics.csv") |> mutate(run = lab)) |>
    mutate(run = factor(run, levels = runs),
           lift_lo = pr_auc_lo / base_rate, lift_hi = pr_auc_hi / base_rate) |>
    ggplot(aes(factor(horizon), pr_lift, colour = run)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lift_lo, ymax = lift_hi),
                    position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#56B4E9", "#D55E00", "#E69F00")) +
    labs(x = "Horizon H (minutes)", y = "PR-AUC / base rate (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

#### Preprocessing for the model

The data are **split by day first**, and every step that learns anything from the
data is then fitted on the training days only and applied unchanged to the
validation and test days. This keeps the test period completely out of the model.

1. **Split by day.** Neighbouring minutes are almost identical, so a random split of
   minutes would put near-copies of the same moment in both training and test sets.
   We split by whole day and keep time order: the earliest days for training, the next
   day for validation, and the latest days (about 30 %) for testing. Bank uses 6 / 1 / 3
   days and Telecom 10 / 1 / 4. The validation day is used for early stopping and for
   choosing the alarm threshold.
2. **Clean the telemetry** as described in @tbl-cleaning: keep series observed on every
   training day, drop series mostly missing on training days, and fill gaps from past
   values only.
3. **Scale.** Each feature is centred on its training median and divided by its
   training interquartile range (IQR), then clipped to $\pm 10$. KPIs are heavy-tailed,
   and the median and IQR are not pulled around by extreme values.
4. **Select features.** Of the cleaned features (1,567 for Bank, 1,231 for Telecom), we
   keep the $k = 128$ with the highest ANOVA $F$-statistic between positive and
   negative training minutes.
5. **Build windows.** Each usable minute $t$ becomes one $60 \times 128$ input: the 60
   minutes of scaled telemetry ending at $t$.
6. **Balance the training set.** Every positive training window is kept and negatives
   are randomly subsampled to five per positive; the loss also gives positives a weight
   equal to the negative-to-positive ratio. The validation and test sets are not
   resampled, so they keep the real, rare positive rate.

| Step | Learned from | Applied to |
|---|---|---|
| Series kept (observed on every day, ≤ 80 % missing) | training days | all days |
| Gap-fill limit per series; median for leftover gaps | training days | all days |
| Gap filling | past values in the same day only | all days |
| Scaling (median, IQR) | training days | all days |
| Feature selection (ANOVA $F$) | training days and their labels | all days |
| Negative subsampling, positive-class weight | training days | training only |
| Early stopping, alarm threshold | validation day | not applied to data |
| Test-day labels | not used | scoring only |

: What each preprocessing step is fitted on. {#tbl-fitted-on}

```{r, echo=TRUE}
bind_rows(Bank    = res("bank",    "chrono-level", "split.csv"),
          Telecom = res("telecom", "chrono-level", "split.csv"), .id = "System") |>
  filter(horizon == 5) |>
  mutate(Split = str_to_title(split),
         Days  = str_replace_all(days, "20(20|21)-", ""),
         `Positive share` = pct(positive / windows)) |>
  select(System, Split, Days, Windows = windows, Positive = positive,
         `Positive share`, `Tensor shape` = shape) |>
  kable(caption = "Data after preprocessing, chronological split, 5-minute horizon. The training set is balanced to 5 negatives per positive; validation and test keep the true rate.")
```

#### Evaluation

Because failures are rare, accuracy is not useful: a model that never raises an alarm
is 95 % accurate at $H = 5$. We report:

- **PR-AUC** (area under the precision–recall curve). A model that guesses at random
  scores the **base rate**, the share of positive minutes, so we also report the
  **lift**, PR-AUC divided by the base rate. A lift of 1 means no skill. The 95 %
  interval comes from resampling 60-minute blocks of the test set; if it includes the
  base rate, the model cannot be distinguished from guessing.
- **ROC-AUC**, where 0.5 means no skill.
- **Faults caught**: the share of faults with at least one alarm in the $H$ minutes
  before they start.
- **False alarms per day**: separate bursts of alarms with no fault following them.
  A Telecom "day" is the 6 hours of recorded telemetry.

PR-AUC and ROC-AUC measure how well the model *ranks* minutes and need no threshold.
To turn probabilities into alarms, the threshold is set on the validation day so that
the model would alarm on about 2 % of minutes (30 alarm-minutes per 24 hours). We also
report the share of test minutes that actually cross this threshold. If it is far
from 2 %, the model's scores have shifted between the validation and test days, and
the fault and false-alarm counts mostly reflect that shift rather than skill.

#### Bank

##### Training

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.6}
#| label: fig-bank-training
#| fig-cap: "Training loss and validation PR-AUC by epoch for each horizon (Bank, chronological split). The dot marks the epoch whose weights were kept."
plot_history("bank")
```

Training is fast: the balanced training set has only a few thousand windows, and each
horizon finishes in a few seconds. Training loss falls steadily, but validation PR-AUC
peaks early, between epochs 1 and 6, so early stopping ends every run within 10 epochs
(@fig-bank-training). On the validation day the model does find some signal: at
$H = 10$ its best validation PR-AUC is 0.24 against a base rate of 0.10, and at
$H = 30$ it is 0.58 against 0.28.

##### Results on the test days

```{r, echo=TRUE}
show_metrics("bank", "chrono-level") |>
  kable(caption = "LSTM on the Bank test days (2021-03-23 to 03-25), chronological split.")
```

On the three test days the LSTM ranks minutes **slightly better than chance at the
middle horizons, but not reliably**. At $H = 3$ to $15$ PR-AUC is above the base rate
(lift 1.2–2.6) and ROC-AUC reaches 0.55–0.63, but every 95 % interval still includes
the base rate. At $H = 1$ and $H = 30$ there is no skill at all.

The model also **raises no alarms**: on every horizon, the test scores stay below the
threshold chosen on the validation day, so none of the 43 test faults is flagged.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
#| label: fig-bank-timeline
#| fig-cap: "Predicted failure probability on the three Bank test days at H = 5. Red lines mark fault onsets; the dashed line is the alarm threshold chosen on the validation day."
plot_timeline("bank", "Bank", "2021-03-23")
```

@fig-bank-timeline shows why. The predicted probability moves in slow waves over hours
rather than rising in the minutes before each fault, and the whole curve sits lower
than on the validation day.

##### What the model is picking up

The features ranked highest by the $F$-test are disk metrics on the two `IG` servers
(used, available and total space) and connection counts on `Mysql01`. @fig-bank-drift
shows the daily level of the top four.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2}
#| label: fig-bank-drift
#| fig-cap: "Daily mean of the four top-ranked Bank features, in units of training IQR from the training median. Shading shows the split each day belongs to."
plot_drift("bank", "\\|\\|OSLinux-OSLinux_FILESYSTEM_-tomcat_")
```

Used disk space grows steadily across the training days, and the share of positive
minutes also differs from day to day: 0 % on the fault-free 03-05 and up to 9 % on
03-09. A slowly drifting feature can therefore look predictive just because it tells
the days apart. Within a single day, used disk space on `IG02` is only about a quarter
of a standard deviation higher before faults than at other times. The $F$-test ranks
these features highly, and the LSTM learns them, mostly because of differences
*between* days rather than warning signs *before* each fault.

The test days stay inside the training range for these features, but the mix of
inputs still shifts: 2.9 % of scaled test values are clipped at $\pm 10$, against 0.5 %
on the training days. That is enough to move the model's scores below the validation
threshold.

##### Checking the explanation

Two further experiments test whether the signal comes from day-level differences:

- **Cross-validation.** Each pair of consecutive days is held out once as the test set
  (5 folds), so training always includes days from both ends of March. All cleaning,
  scaling and feature selection are re-fitted inside each fold, and the out-of-fold
  predictions are pooled before scoring. Because some training days come *after* the
  test days, this is a diagnostic, not a realistic forecast.
- **Change inputs.** Each window has its own median subtracted, feature by feature, so
  the model sees only how the metrics change within the hour and not their level.
  Features are also ranked on within-day variation, which removes day-to-day drift
  from the selection.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
#| label: fig-bank-lift
#| fig-cap: "Bank: PR-AUC lift over the base rate with 95 % intervals, for both splits and both input types. A lift of 1 (dashed line) means no skill."
plot_lift("bank")
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
show_metrics("bank", "cv-level") |>
  kable(caption = "Bank with cross-validation (5 folds, all 10 days tested once), level inputs.")
```

The results support the explanation (@fig-bank-lift):

- With **cross-validation and level inputs**, the LSTM is consistently above chance:
  lift 1.2–1.5 at every horizon, ROC-AUC 0.55–0.60, and at four of the six horizons
  the interval excludes the base rate.
- With **change inputs**, which remove the day-level information, this advantage
  disappears: lift is 0.94–1.05 at every horizon from 3 to 30 minutes.
- With the **chronological split**, neither input type gives a reliable signal.

The fault counts in the cross-validation table look better (21–33 % of faults caught),
but the thresholds there alarm on 12–24 % of minutes instead of 2 %; except at
$H = 1$, random alarms at that rate would catch as many faults or more.

##### What the Bank data reveal

For Bank, the LSTM **does not find reliable warning signs in the hour before an
injected fault**. The little skill it shows comes from slow differences between days,
such as disk usage that grows over the recording. That information helps when training
and test days are mixed, but not when the model has to predict later days from earlier
ones, which is how it would be used in practice.

#### Telecom

Telecom is a harder setting: 15 six-hour days, 51 faults instead of 136, and three
times as many components. The chronological split trains on 10 days (04-11, 04-20 to
04-23 and 05-22 to 05-26, with 29 faults), validates on 05-27 (8 faults) and tests on
05-28 to 05-31 (14 faults). Four of the training days have no faults at all.

##### Training

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.6}
#| label: fig-telecom-training
#| fig-cap: "Training loss and validation PR-AUC by epoch for each horizon (Telecom, chronological split)."
plot_history("telecom")
```

As with Bank, validation PR-AUC peaks within the first few epochs (between epochs 1
and 8) and early stopping ends every run within 12 epochs. The validation day is
unusually fault-heavy (13 % of minutes positive at $H = 5$), so validation PR-AUC
looks high; relative to its base rate the gain is modest, for example 0.41 against
0.27 at $H = 10$.

##### Results on the test days

```{r, echo=TRUE}
show_metrics("telecom", "chrono-level") |>
  kable(caption = "LSTM on the Telecom test days (2020-05-28 to 05-31), chronological split. A day is 6 hours of telemetry.")
```

On the Telecom test days the LSTM is **no better than chance** at any horizon:
lift is 1.0–1.3, ROC-AUC stays between 0.46 and 0.54, and every interval includes the
base rate. With only 14 test faults, the intervals are also much wider than for Bank.

The alarms fail in the opposite way to Bank. The validation threshold is *too low*
for the test days, so the model alarms on 53–76 % of test minutes at $H = 3$ to $15$
instead of about 2 %. It catches 7–8 of the 14 faults, but only because it is
alarming most of the time.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
#| label: fig-telecom-timeline
#| fig-cap: "Predicted failure probability on the four Telecom test days at H = 5 (00:00–05:59 each day). Red lines mark fault onsets; the dashed line is the alarm threshold chosen on the validation day."
plot_timeline("telecom", "Telecom", "2020-05-28")
```

##### What the model is picking up

The top-ranked Telecom features are memory metrics of host `os_021` (used and
available memory, in absolute and percentage terms), followed by session and memory
metrics of database `db_002` and host `os_019`.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2}
#| label: fig-telecom-drift
#| fig-cap: "Daily mean of the four top-ranked Telecom features (memory on host os_021), in units of training IQR from the training median."
plot_drift("telecom", "\\|\\|node\\.")
```

@fig-telecom-drift shows the same pattern as Bank, in a stronger form. Memory use on
`os_021` is far below normal on 04-11 and 05-26, which are the two training days with
the most faults (10 % and 16 % of minutes positive), and at or slightly above normal
on the four fault-free days. The $F$-test therefore ranks this feature at the top, although
within a day it differs between pre-fault and other minutes by only about a tenth of a
standard deviation. The validation day breaks the pattern: it is fault-heavy but has
*high* memory use, and 13 % of its scaled values are clipped, against 3 % on the
training and test days. A threshold chosen on such a day does not transfer.

##### Checking the explanation

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
#| label: fig-telecom-lift
#| fig-cap: "Telecom: PR-AUC lift over the base rate with 95 % intervals, for both splits and both input types."
plot_lift("telecom")
```

Running the same two experiments (8 cross-validation folds) gives no consistent
signal (@fig-telecom-lift). With level inputs, cross-validation lift is 0.9–1.2; with
change inputs it is 0.9–1.6, and every interval includes the base rate. The one
exception is the chronological split with change inputs at $H = 1$ (lift 6.1, ROC-AUC
0.76, 3 of 14 faults caught). That result rests on 12 positive test minutes and
concerns the single minute before the recorded start, where the fault may already be
under way, so we treat it as a lead for future work rather than a finding.

##### What the Telecom data reveal

Telecom confirms the Bank result. The LSTM latches onto features that separate
fault-heavy days from quiet ones, here memory use on one host, and this does not
carry over to new days. With 51 faults in total and 14 in the test period, Telecom
also shows how little data a fault-prediction study has once it is counted in events
rather than minutes.

#### Studying the LSTM

The results so far describe what the model achieves. This part looks at *how* the
LSTM behaves: whether it uses its memory, how sensitive it is to its settings, what
its gates do, and which inputs drive its predictions. All experiments use the
chronological split, level inputs and a horizon of $H = 10$ minutes, a middle horizon
where about 10 % of minutes are positive in both systems. Each setting is trained once
and scored on the validation day and on the test days.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
study <- function(system, file)
  read_csv(file.path("results", system, "study", file), show_col_types = FALSE)
both <- function(file)
  bind_rows(Bank = study("bank", file), Telecom = study("telecom", file), .id = "system")
```

##### Memory length and model size

The defining feature of an LSTM is its ability to remember. If warning signs built up
over the hour before a fault, a longer look-back window should help. We varied the
look-back from $L = 1$ minute, which gives the LSTM a single time step and so no
sequence at all, up to $L = 120$ minutes. We also varied the number of hidden units
from $d = 8$ to $d = 128$, which changes the number of parameters from about 4,400 to
about 132,000.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.2}
#| label: fig-study-settings
#| fig-cap: "PR-AUC lift on the validation day and on the test days for different look-back lengths (left) and hidden sizes (right), H = 10. Test intervals are 95 % block-bootstrap intervals; the dashed line is no skill."
bind_rows(both("lookback.csv") |> mutate(setting = "Look-back L (minutes)", value = lookback),
          both("hidden.csv")   |> mutate(setting = "Hidden units d",        value = hidden)) |>
  transmute(system, setting, value = factor(value),
            Validation = val_lift, Test = test_lift,
            lo = test_lo / test_base, hi = test_hi / test_base) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Validation, Test), names_to = "data", values_to = "lift") |>
  mutate(lo = if_else(data == "Test", lo, NA_real_),
         hi = if_else(data == "Test", hi, NA_real_)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, lift, colour = data)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
                  na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  facet_grid(system ~ setting, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Test = "#D55E00", Validation = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "PR-AUC / base rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Memory does not help** (@fig-study-settings, left). On Bank, an LSTM that sees only
the current minute ($L = 1$) reaches a test lift of 1.43, about the same as with the
full hour ($L = 60$, lift 1.47); every other look-back falls between 1.15 and 1.35.
On Telecom the test lift is between 0.85 and 1.07 for every look-back. In both
systems the model does as well without a sequence as with one, so the order of the
minutes adds nothing that the current readings do not already contain.

**Model size does not matter much either** (@fig-study-settings, right). On Bank the
test lift ranges from 1.09 to 1.47 across hidden sizes; on Telecom from 0.99 to 1.78,
and all of these intervals include the base rate.

**Validation scores do not predict test scores.** Every setting looks useful on the
validation day (lift 2.3 to 3.4 on Bank, 1.2 to 2.4 on Telecom), yet test lift is much
lower. Choosing the setting with the best validation score would have picked
$L = 30$ for Bank (test lift 1.18) and $d = 8$ for Telecom (test lift 1.09), neither of
which is the best on the test days. The validation day, one day just after training,
is not representative of the later test days.

##### Stability across random seeds

```{r, echo=TRUE}
both("seeds.csv") |>
  group_by(System = system) |>
  summarise(Runs = n(),
            `Validation lift, mean (SD)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", mean(val_lift), sd(val_lift)),
            `Test lift, mean (SD)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", mean(test_lift), sd(test_lift)),
            `Test lift range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(test_lift), max(test_lift)),
            `Test ROC-AUC range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(test_roc), max(test_roc))) |>
  kable(caption = "The default LSTM (L = 60, d = 64) trained with five random seeds, H = 10.")
```

Training the same model with five different random seeds changes the result as much
as changing its settings. On Bank the test lift ranges from 0.87 to 1.48 (mean 1.23),
so one seed is worse than random guessing and another is among the best runs of the
whole study. On Telecom it ranges from 1.01 to 1.34 (mean 1.14). Any single run,
including the results reported above, should be read with this spread in mind.

##### Inside the LSTM: the gates

Because the gate equations in @eq-lstm are explicit, we can compute the gate values
the trained model produces. @fig-study-gates shows the forget, input and output gates,
averaged over all hidden units and over the test windows, at each minute of the
60-minute window. Windows before a fault and other windows are shown separately.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.6}
#| label: fig-study-gates
#| fig-cap: "Mean gate activation at each minute of the look-back window (0 = the current minute), default model, test windows, H = 10."
both("gates.csv") |>
  mutate(gate = str_to_title(gate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(minute, mean, colour = gate, linetype = label)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~system) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Forget = "#D55E00", Input = "#009E73", Output = "#0072B2")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.3, 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "Minute in window", y = "Mean gate value", colour = "Gate", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The gates explain why memory length does not matter. In Bank the forget gate averages
about 0.39 at every minute. Because the cell state is multiplied by the forget gate at
each step ($c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + \dots$), information from $k$ minutes ago is
scaled by roughly $0.39^k$: about 15 % survives two minutes and less than 1 % survives
five. The trained Bank LSTM has learned to **forget almost immediately**, so in practice
it acts on the last minute or two. In Telecom all three gates stay close to 0.5, which
is the value of the sigmoid at zero: the network has barely moved away from its
starting point before early stopping ends training, again consistent with there being
little to learn. In both systems the gate values before faults and at other times are
almost identical.

##### What the predictions depend on

To see which inputs drive the predictions, we computed the gradient of the model's
output with respect to every input value and multiplied it by that value
(input × gradient). Large values mean that changing the input would change the
prediction. Averaging over features gives the importance of each minute of the window
(@fig-study-saliency); averaging over minutes gives the importance of each feature.

```{r, echo=TRUE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.4}
#| label: fig-study-saliency
#| fig-cap: "Mean |input × gradient| for each minute of the look-back window (log scale), default model, test windows, H = 10."
both("saliency_time.csv") |>
  ggplot(aes(minute, saliency, linetype = label)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~system) +
  labs(x = "Minute in window (0 = the current minute)", y = "Mean |input x gradient|",
       linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

In Bank the current minute alone carries 57 % to 64 % of the total importance and the
last three minutes 73 % to 80 %, matching the short memory seen in the gates. In
Telecom the importance is spread a little more widely, but the last five minutes still
carry about half of it. Windows before faults and other windows look the same.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
both("saliency_feature.csv") |>
  group_by(system) |> slice_head(n = 8) |>
  mutate(Rank = row_number(),
         Component = str_extract(feature, "^[^|]+"),
         KPI = str_remove(feature, "^[^|]+\\|\\|") |>
           str_remove("^OSLinux-OSLinux_|^Mysql-MySQL_3306_|^redis-Redis_6379_")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(System = system, Rank, Component, KPI) |>
  kable(caption = "The eight features with the largest mean |input x gradient|, default model, H = 10.")
```

The most influential Bank features are revealing: host **uptime** on three Tomcat
servers, Redis's internal **clock** (`lru_clock`) and its **cumulative** command count,
and used disk space. All of these grow steadily with time, so they tell the model
*when* a minute is, not whether a fault is coming. This is the same day-level
information that the cross-validation and change-input experiments pointed to, now
seen directly inside the model. In Telecom the most influential features are memory
use on host `os_014`, Redis key counts and database load, again slowly varying levels
rather than sudden changes.

##### What the LSTM study shows

The LSTM's defining strength, a long memory controlled by learned gates, goes unused
on these data. Trained on OpenRCA telemetry, it learns to forget within a minute or
two, relies on the current readings, and leans on features that track elapsed time.
This is a sensible response to the data rather than a failure of training: as
@fig-onset-profile showed, the telemetry does not change before faults, so there is
no long-range pattern for the memory to hold.

#### Comparing the two systems

```{r, echo=TRUE}
bind_rows(Bank    = res("bank",    "chrono-level", "metrics.csv"),
          Telecom = res("telecom", "chrono-level", "metrics.csv"), .id = "System") |>
  group_by(System) |>
  summarise(`Lift range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(pr_lift), max(pr_lift)),
            `ROC-AUC range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(roc_auc), max(roc_auc)),
            `Horizons with CI above base rate` =
              sprintf("%d of %d", sum(pr_auc_lo > base_rate), n()),
            `Test faults` = first(n_events)) |>
  kable(caption = "Chronological split, level inputs: summary over the six horizons.")
```

Across two systems with different domains, components and fault types, the picture
is the same: on later days the LSTM ranks minutes no better than chance, its scores
shift between days so that a fixed alarm threshold either never fires (Bank) or fires
most of the time (Telecom), and the features it relies on mainly tell days apart.

### Conclusion

**Key findings.**

- An LSTM given the last 60 minutes of metric telemetry **did not reliably predict
  injected failures** in either OpenRCA system when tested on later days. Across
  horizons from 1 to 30 minutes, PR-AUC stayed within the uncertainty of the base rate
  for both Bank (43 test faults) and Telecom (14 test faults).
- The modest skill the model showed came from **differences between days** (disk
  usage growing over the Bank recording, memory use on one Telecom host) rather than
  warning signs in the minutes before a fault. When the inputs were reduced to
  within-hour changes, the skill disappeared.
- The model's output **shifted from day to day**, so an alarm threshold tuned on one
  day never fired on the Bank test days and fired most of the time on the Telecom test
  days.
- The telemetry itself **changes at the start of a fault, not before it**. Averaged
  over all faults, the metrics move no more in the hour before a fault than at quiet
  times, and then jump in the first minutes after it.
- The LSTM's memory **went unused**. A model that sees only the current minute did as
  well as one that sees the whole hour. In Bank the trained forget gate keeps less than
  1 % of the cell state after five minutes and the last three minutes carry about
  three quarters of the input importance; in Telecom the gates barely moved from their
  starting values. The most influential inputs were counters and clocks such
  as host uptime, which encode elapsed time rather than system health.
- Results varied as much between **random seeds** as between settings, and the
  setting that looked best on the validation day was never the best on the test days.

**Implications.**

- For **choosing an LSTM**, its advantage depends on the data containing patterns
  that unfold over time. When warning signs do not exist, as in these injected-fault
  data, the gates learn to discard the past and the LSTM behaves like a model of the
  current minute, with extra parameters and extra variance from training.
- For **this kind of data**, minute-level early warning appears very hard. Many
  injected faults (CPU load, network loss, latency) are switched on abruptly, so the
  metrics may not change until the fault starts. Benchmarks such as OpenRCA, built for
  root-cause analysis, may be better suited to detecting and diagnosing failures than
  to predicting them.
- For **evaluating failure prediction**, the design choices matter as much as the
  model. Splitting by day, testing on later days, fitting all preprocessing on the
  training days, and counting results in fault events rather than minutes all made the
  results less flattering but more honest. A random split of minutes, or preprocessing
  fitted on all days, would overstate how well the model works.
- For **deploying** such a model, a fixed threshold is not enough: scores would need
  to be recalibrated regularly, for example against a rolling window of recent data.
